title: Concentrations in a two compartment model

segs.text: Module two, objective six. Predicting concentrations after an I V bolus in a two compartment model. The plasma concentration is the sum of two falling first order terms, a fast one for distribution and a slow one for elimination. A and B are their intercepts on the log concentration axis, in milligrams per liter, and alpha and beta are their slopes, in per hour. She said, the A or alpha and the B or beta, those are what we call our microconstants. She gives you these four numbers, or the equation that contains them, and you substitute; you do not derive them.

card.m: A, B: intercepts, mg/L; a (alpha), b (beta): slopes, hr<sup>−1</sup>
given: A, B, a, b, or the equation

segs.text: Why does each term behave as it does? Late in the curve the plasma level falls on one straight line, the beta term alone, so its intercept is B and its slope beta, and the elimination half-life comes from beta alone. Early, the curve lies above that line, and the difference is the alpha term, with intercept A and slope alpha. Distribution is faster than elimination, so alpha is always the larger constant and the alpha term shrinks to almost nothing within the first hours; A and B can be either way round. Both intercepts are in proportion to the dose, so doubling the dose doubles A, B and every concentration, while alpha and beta do not change.

card.m: late: Be<sup>−bt</sup> alone → beta half-life from b
a > b always; A, B either way
dose × 2: A, B, every C<sub>p</sub> × 2; a, b unchanged

segs.text: The relation is C p equals A e to the minus alpha t plus B e to the minus beta t. At time zero both exponentials equal one, so C p zero equals A plus B. The beta half-life is zero point six nine three over beta, the first order half-life applied to the elimination phase; beta is on the bottom, so a smaller beta gives a longer half-life. Divide by beta directly. She said, Do not get all complicated. The overall rate constant k is a different number from beta, so zero point six nine three over k is not the beta half-life.

Her practice problem gives theophylline as C p equals twelve e to the minus five point eight t, plus eighteen e to the minus zero point one six t, and asks the plasma level three hours after the dose. The first check is the order of the terms: five point eight is much larger than zero point one six, so the first term is distribution and the second elimination. At time zero the level is thirty milligrams per liter. The beta half-life is four point three three hours. By three hours the distribution term is effectively zero, so the level is the elimination term alone, eleven point one four milligrams per liter.

The same four numbers give the rate constants of the model. k, the overall elimination rate constant, describes elimination from the central compartment. It is larger than beta, because in the elimination phase drug returning from the tissue enters the plasma, so the plasma level falls more slowly than k alone would make it. k equals alpha times beta times the sum A plus B, over the cross term, A times beta plus B times alpha. k two one, tissue to central, is the cross term over A plus B. k one two, central to tissue, is A times B times the square of beta minus alpha, over A plus B times the cross term.

card.m: k: elimination from the central compartment, hr<sup>−1</sup>
k > b: drug returning from tissue slows the fall
cross term: Ab + Ba, each intercept × the other phase slope; work it out once

segs.text: The central volume, V p, is the dose divided by A plus B, which is D zero over C p zero, the same idea as V D in one compartment. At the same dose, a larger A plus B means a smaller V p. When a dose and an area under the curve are given instead, V p equals D zero over k times A U C. The tissue volume, V t, equals V p times k one two over k two one: the faster drug moves out to the tissue compared with back, the larger the tissue volume.

Her in class sheet gives a two hundred fifty milligram bolus, A eight point four five and B five point three two milligrams per liter, alpha two point one eight and beta zero point one one four per hour. The beta half-life is six point zero eight hours, and C p zero is thirteen point seven seven milligrams per liter. At four hours the alpha term is about one thousandth of a milligram per liter, so the level is nearly all beta term, three point three seven milligrams per liter. The central volume is eighteen point one six liters.

For the rate constants, the cross term comes first, twelve point five six. Then k is zero point two seven two per hour, more than twice beta, which is zero point one one four per hour, so k and beta are clearly different numbers. k two one is zero point nine one two per hour, and k one two is one point one zero nine per hour.

card.m: k 0.272 vs b 0.114 hr<sup>−1</sup>: k is not b

segs.text: She gives the equation, or A, B, alpha and beta, and does not say two compartment. Four parts recur in this order: the elimination half-life, the initial concentration, a concentration at a stated hour, and the central volume. The elimination half-life is always zero point six nine three over the smaller constant, beta; using alpha, or calculating k first, is the usual mistake. She said, It will be written as beta half-life, because I am going to ask you for either the beta half-life or the elimination half-life, so that there is no confusion. The overall elimination rate constant means k, not beta. Only her in-class sheet adds k, k one two and k two one to those four.
